Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette:
Leilani was twenty years old, but she felt much older. She was an auditor for a mid-sized firm in Honolulu, a job she had taken straight out of community college because it was quiet, predictable, and required almost no interaction with strangers. She had been working there for just over a year when the stalking began, and now, nine months after it ended, she could not shake the feeling that her life had been permanently hollowed out.

The stalking had started subtly. A man she had briefly dated twice began appearing wherever she went—outside her apartment, at the grocery store, in the parking lot of her office. At first she told herself she was being paranoid, but then the notes started appearing under her windshield wiper, always the same phrase: *I see you*. The police were called, a restraining order was obtained, but he never stopped. He was arrested only after he broke into her apartment while she was at work and left a photograph of her sleeping on her own pillow, taken through her bedroom window the night before. That was the moment she understood that nowhere was safe. The trial had ended three months ago, and he was now in prison, but the sense of violation had not receded. It had only calcified.

Leilani had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, a place where threats hid in plain sight. She was certain that if she let her guard down for even a moment, something terrible would happen again. This hypervigilance had become the background hum of her days. She scanned every room she entered for exits, for faces that lingered too long, for anyone who seemed to be watching her. In the office, she insisted on a desk that faced the door, and she flinched every time a coworker approached from behind. She had stopped taking the elevator altogether because the enclosed space made her feel trapped; she walked the six flights of stairs twice a day, arriving at her desk breathless and sweaty, but at least she could see the full staircase before she entered it.

The most insidious change, however, was the way she had turned against herself. Leilani had developed a punishing internal narrative that whispered she deserved what had happened. She had gone on those two dates, she had been friendly, she had smiled too much—surely that meant she had invited the attention. She told herself she was weak for not sensing the danger earlier, for not being smarter, for not fighting back when he broke in. She had come to believe that she deserved to suffer, and so she refused herself any relief. When her mother invited her to a weekend barbecue with cousins, she said no, not because she was afraid of the crowd—though she was—but because she felt she had no right to enjoy herself. She actively avoided any situation that might make her feel happy or hopeful, as if happiness were a betrayal of the trauma she had survived. She had stopped listening to music she used to love, stopped watching her favorite shows, stopped accepting invitations to anything that might resemble joy.

The avoidance had become a full-time job. She rarely left her apartment except for work and essential errands, and even then she planned her routes meticulously. She never went out after dark. She had stopped seeing friends entirely, and her only regular contact outside of work was a weekly phone call with her mother, which she often cut short. Her social world had shrunk to the size of her cubicle and her studio apartment. She knew this was not sustainable, but the thought of going out—of being seen, of being vulnerable—filled her with a dread so physical that her stomach would clench and her palms would sweat. She was certain that if she let herself feel even a moment of peace, she would be punished for it.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was not a crisis, but a quiet moment of exhaustion. She had been sitting in her apartment on a Saturday afternoon, staring at the wall, and she realized she could not remember the last time she had felt anything other than fear or guilt. She had read about PTSD online, and the description of hypervigilance and avoidance had felt like a description of her own life. She was terrified that she would never feel normal again, that the man who had stalked her had stolen not just her sense of safety but her entire future. She came to therapy hoping—though she barely dared to admit it—that she might one day leave her apartment without scanning the street first, that she might hear a door close without her heart stopping, that she might, somehow, believe she deserved to be okay.
